questions.question: Which Unity method is called once when the GameObject is first initialized, even if the component is disabled?
options: Update
Start
Awake
OnEnable
questions.explanation: Awake is called once when the GameObject is initialized, before Start, even if the component itself is disabled. It will not fire if the GameObject is inactive in the hierarchy.

questions.question: What is the correct order of these Unity lifecycle methods on startup?
options: Start → Awake → OnEnable
Awake → Start → OnEnable
Awake → OnEnable → Start
OnEnable → Awake → Start
questions.explanation: Awake fires first, then OnEnable when the component becomes active, then Start before the first frame update.

questions.question: When is OnDestroy called?
options: When the component is disabled
When the scene is paused
When the GameObject or component is destroyed
At the end of every frame
questions.explanation: OnDestroy is called when the GameObject or component is being destroyed, either via Destroy() or when the scene unloads.

questions.question: What is the difference between FixedUpdate and Update?
options: FixedUpdate runs faster than Update
FixedUpdate runs on a consistent time step, Update runs every frame
Update is used for physics, FixedUpdate for input
There is no difference
questions.explanation: FixedUpdate runs on a fixed time step independent of frame rate, making it suitable for physics. Update runs once per rendered frame.

questions.question: What is LateUpdate used for?
options: Running logic after physics
Running logic after all Update calls have finished
Running logic on a fixed time step
Running logic only once
questions.explanation: LateUpdate runs after all Update methods have been called that frame. Commonly used for camera follow logic so it runs after the target has moved.

questions.question: How many times can OnEnable fire on a single component during a session?
options: Once — same as Awake
Twice at most
Once per scene load
Every time the component or GameObject is activated
questions.explanation: Unlike Awake, OnEnable fires every time the component or its GameObject becomes active. If you disable and re-enable an object repeatedly, OnEnable fires each time.

questions.question: Does OnDisable fire when a scene is unloaded?
options: No, only Destroy triggers OnDisable
Yes, because all objects are deactivated during unload
Only if the object has DontDestroyOnLoad
Only if the component was enabled at the time
questions.explanation: When a scene unloads, OnDisable is called as part of the destruction sequence for every active component, followed by OnDestroy.
questions.hint: OnDisable is part of the destruction sequence — it fires before OnDestroy.

questions.question: Can Awake be called on a disabled component?
options: No, the component must be enabled
No, the GameObject must be active
Yes, as long as the GameObject is active in the hierarchy
Yes, regardless of the GameObject's state
questions.explanation: Awake is called when the GameObject is active in the hierarchy, even if the component itself is disabled. It will not fire if the GameObject is inactive.
questions.hint: Awake fires based on the GameObject being active, not the component being enabled.

questions.question: If a component is disabled at startup, when does Start run?
options: Never — Start only runs if the component was enabled from the beginning
Immediately when the component is first enabled
On the frame after the component is first enabled
At the same time as Awake
questions.explanation: Start is deferred — it runs on the frame after the component is first enabled, not the same frame it becomes active.
questions.hint: Start is deferred — it runs on the frame after the component is first enabled.

questions.question: You need Script A's Awake to always run before Script B's Awake. What is the correct way to guarantee this?
options: Put Script A higher in the hierarchy
Use Script Execution Order in Project Settings
Call Script A's Awake manually from Script B
Use a static constructor in Script A
questions.explanation: Script Execution Order (Edit > Project Settings > Script Execution Order) lets you explicitly define the order scripts initialise across the project.
questions.hint: There is a setting in Project Settings specifically for this.

questions.question: What happens if you call `Destroy(gameObject)` inside Awake?
options: It throws an exception
The GameObject is destroyed immediately before Start runs
The GameObject is marked for destruction and destroyed at the end of the frame
Nothing, Destroy is ignored in Awake
questions.explanation: Destroy is never immediate unless you use DestroyImmediate. The object is marked and destroyed at the end of the current frame, so other callbacks within the same frame may still execute.

questions.question: What is the difference between `Destroy` and `DestroyImmediate`?
options: They are identical
DestroyImmediate skips OnDestroy
Destroy queues destruction for end of frame, DestroyImmediate destroys instantly
Destroy only works on components, DestroyImmediate on GameObjects
questions.explanation: Destroy queues the object for destruction at the end of the frame. DestroyImmediate destroys it instantly and is generally only safe to use in editor scripts.

questions.question: Why should you avoid calling `FindObjectOfType` in Update?
options: It only works in Awake
It throws an exception at runtime
It searches the entire scene every call and is very expensive
It returns null in Update
questions.explanation: FindObjectOfType scans all objects in the scene every time it's called. Doing this every frame causes significant performance overhead.

questions.question: What does `DontDestroyOnLoad` do?
options: Prevents the GameObject from being destroyed by Destroy()
Keeps the GameObject alive when a new scene is loaded
Makes the GameObject persist between editor sessions
Prevents the GameObject from being disabled
questions.explanation: DontDestroyOnLoad moves the GameObject to a special scene that persists across scene loads, commonly used for managers and audio.

questions.question: What does `GetComponent<T>()` return if the component is not found?
options: It throws a NullReferenceException
It returns a default struct value
It returns null
It logs a warning and returns a new instance
questions.explanation: GetComponent returns null if the component is not found. You should null-check the result before using it.

questions.question: Where should you read player input — Update or FixedUpdate?
options: FixedUpdate, because it's more reliable
Update, because input is sampled once per frame
Either — there is no difference
LateUpdate, so it runs after physics
questions.explanation: Input is sampled once per rendered frame. Reading it in FixedUpdate can miss or double-count presses because FixedUpdate may run multiple times or zero times per frame.

questions.question: A destroyed Unity object evaluates to `null` in an `if` check. Why is this?
options: C# sets the reference to null automatically
Unity overrides the == operator on UnityEngine.Object
The GC collects it immediately
It throws an exception instead
questions.explanation: UnityEngine.Object overrides == so that a destroyed object compares equal to null, even though the C# object still exists in memory until GC collects it.
questions.hint: Unity overrides the == operator on UnityEngine.Object.

questions.question: Which of the following are true about ScriptableObjects?
options: They are assets that live in the project
They run Update every frame
They are good for storing shared data
They must be attached to a GameObject
questions.explanation: ScriptableObjects are project assets used to store shared data. They don't run per-frame methods and don't need a GameObject.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a ScriptableObject and a plain [Serializable] class?
options: Serializable classes can be assets, ScriptableObjects cannot
ScriptableObjects exist as shared assets, serializable classes are embedded copies inside their owner
There is no difference
ScriptableObjects cannot hold data
questions.explanation: A plain serializable class is embedded and serialized inside its owner — each object gets its own copy. A ScriptableObject is a standalone asset that can be shared and referenced by many objects.
questions.hint: A [Serializable] class is embedded inside its owner. A ScriptableObject is a standalone asset.

questions.question: You modify a ScriptableObject asset's data at runtime during Play Mode in the editor. What happens when you exit Play Mode?
options: Changes are lost — the asset reverts to its pre-Play-Mode values
Changes are saved permanently to the asset
It depends on whether you called AssetDatabase.SaveAssets()
Changes are saved only if the asset is marked Dirty
questions.explanation: Unlike MonoBehaviour fields, changes to ScriptableObject assets during Play Mode ARE saved to the asset on disk. This is a common gotcha — it means runtime code can unintentionally corrupt your design data. Use runtime clones (Instantiate) if you need mutable state.
questions.hint: Unlike MonoBehaviour fields, ScriptableObject changes in Play Mode persist to the asset.

questions.question: You have a ScriptableObject that stores mutable game state (e.g. current health). What is the correct approach at runtime?
options: Modify the asset directly — it resets on play
Instantiate a copy of the asset at runtime and modify that
Use DontDestroyOnLoad on the asset
Wrap all writes in #if UNITY_EDITOR
questions.explanation: In the editor, modifying an SO asset directly persists the changes to disk. Always Instantiate() a runtime copy so your changes are isolated and the source asset stays clean.
questions.hint: Instantiate() works on ScriptableObjects too, not just prefabs.

questions.question: What does the `[CreateAssetMenu]` attribute do?
options: Makes the ScriptableObject a singleton
Adds an entry to the Assets > Create menu to create an instance of this asset
Automatically saves the asset on change
Marks the class as serializable
questions.explanation: [CreateAssetMenu] registers the ScriptableObject type in the Assets > Create right-click menu, making it easy for designers to create new instances without touching code.

questions.question: What does `yield return null` do inside a coroutine?
options: Stops the coroutine permanently
Pauses the coroutine until a condition is met
Pauses the coroutine and resumes on the next frame
Pauses the coroutine for one second
questions.explanation: yield return null suspends the coroutine and resumes execution at the start of the next frame.

questions.question: What is the difference between `WaitForSeconds` and `WaitForSecondsRealtime`?
options: They are identical
WaitForSeconds is more accurate
WaitForSeconds is affected by Time.timeScale, WaitForSecondsRealtime is not
WaitForSecondsRealtime only works in editor
questions.explanation: WaitForSeconds respects Time.timeScale — if the game is paused or slowed, so is the wait. WaitForSecondsRealtime uses wall clock time and is unaffected by timeScale.
questions.hint: WaitForSeconds uses scaled time. There is a Realtime variant.

questions.question: What happens to a coroutine when its GameObject is disabled?
options: It pauses and resumes when the GameObject is re-enabled
It continues running in the background
It is stopped and cannot be resumed
It throws an exception
questions.explanation: Disabling a GameObject stops all coroutines running on it. They are not paused — they are stopped entirely and must be restarted manually if needed.
questions.hint: Disabling stops them — they do not pause and resume.

questions.question: Why is it better to cache a `WaitForSeconds` instance rather than creating it with `new` inside the coroutine loop?
options: new WaitForSeconds throws inside coroutines
It avoids a heap allocation every iteration, reducing GC pressure
Cached instances run faster due to Unity optimisation
There is no difference
questions.explanation: Every `new WaitForSeconds(x)` allocates on the heap. In a looping coroutine this creates repeated garbage. Cache it once as a field or static and reuse it.
questions.hint: new allocates on the heap every time. Cache it as a field to avoid repeated allocations.

questions.question: You call `StopAllCoroutines()`. Which coroutines does it stop?
options: All coroutines in the scene
All coroutines on the same MonoBehaviour
Only coroutines started with StartCoroutine on any object
Only the most recently started coroutine
questions.explanation: StopAllCoroutines only stops coroutines running on the MonoBehaviour it is called on. Other MonoBehaviours are unaffected.
questions.hint: StopAllCoroutines only affects the MonoBehaviour it is called on.

questions.question: What return type must a coroutine method have?
options: void
Task
IEnumerator
Coroutine
questions.explanation: Unity coroutines must return IEnumerator. The Coroutine handle returned by StartCoroutine is separate from the method signature itself.

questions.question: How do you wait for another coroutine to finish before continuing?
options: yield return StartCoroutine(OtherRoutine())
await OtherRoutine()
yield return OtherRoutine()
StartCoroutine(OtherRoutine()) with a callback
questions.explanation: yield return StartCoroutine(OtherRoutine()) suspends the outer coroutine until the inner one completes. yield return OtherRoutine() alone does not work correctly.
questions.hint: yield return StartCoroutine() — not just yield return OtherRoutine().

questions.question: Why should Rigidbody movement be applied in FixedUpdate rather than Update?
options: Rigidbody only exists in FixedUpdate
FixedUpdate runs on a fixed time step that matches the physics simulation
Update causes Rigidbody to ignore gravity
Physics only processes input from FixedUpdate
questions.explanation: The physics engine steps at a fixed time interval. Applying forces or velocity in FixedUpdate keeps movement in sync with the simulation. Using Update causes inconsistent results across different frame rates.

questions.question: What does `Physics.Raycast` return?
options: The first collider hit as a Collider reference
True if the ray hit something, with hit data in an out RaycastHit parameter
An array of all colliders along the ray
A RaycastHit or null
questions.explanation: Physics.Raycast returns a bool. Hit information (point, normal, collider, distance) is written to an out RaycastHit that you pass in.

questions.question: What does setting a Rigidbody to `isKinematic = true` do?
options: Disables collision detection entirely
Makes the object ignore gravity only
Removes it from physics simulation while still triggering collisions and triggers
Locks the object's position
questions.explanation: A kinematic Rigidbody is not driven by the physics engine — forces and collisions don't move it. You move it via Transform or MovePosition. It still participates in collision and trigger callbacks.
questions.hint: Forces and collisions will not move a kinematic Rigidbody. You move it manually.
